title: No More Robots 九年历程：发行首款自研 IP——“听起来天真愚蠢，但不知怎地奏效了”
content:
No More Robots' nine-year journey to releasing its first self-developed IP – "This sounds so naive and stupid, but somehow it's working" | GamesIndustry.biz

.
It's been nine years since
Mike Rose set up the indie publisher No More Robots
.
The firm has seen solid success in that time, in part bolstered by a back catalogue that includes the
bike-riding megatitle Descenders
, which was the first game released under the No More Robots name and which is still a huge seller.
Mike Rose, nine years ago  |
Image credit:
Mike Rose
Now, No More Robots is set to release its first self-developed game, the cruise liner simulator Cruise Control, after a major pivot along the way. The title's genesis was a discussion between Rose and Dan Foster, who joined No More Robots to deliver console ports, but brought online multiplayer experience from his time at Team 17. The conversation spawned development of a team-based online shooter, which ultimately took three years and attracted interest from a "big company", says Rose. "Someone who you would know very well."
The future seemed bright - but ultimately the other party pulled out, saying it wasn't the right fit. This was also around the time that
Concord came out and was swiftly pulled from sale
, potentially signalling problems in the online shooter space.
"As you'd imagine, there's no way that we as a tiny company could just launch an online multiplayer shooter by ourselves," Rose says. "Maybe I could just find someone else. But also I was just crushed. It was one of the most unpleasant things I've felt in this industry. And it was from a partner who I massively respect."
Why liner
No More Robots put the shooter project on ice, and Rose had to work out what the five-person development team would work on next. He hit on the idea of Cruise Control. Or, to be specific, the name Cruise Control, followed by a game idea that he knew was "a thing we could make quickly... and it's a genre on PC that we know does well."
No More Robots initially set out to make a shooter before pivoting to create Cruise Control  |
Image credit:
No More Robots
It started as a cruise ship management game in the vein of
games like Two Point Hospital or Two Point Museum
, but has since evolved into more of a puzzle title inspired by
the likes of Mini Motorways
.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, Rose says that releasing a game his own company has made is a very different experience from publishing someone else's work. Despite the higher level of anxiety, the No More Robots boss says the potential upside of Cruise Control doing well is much higher.
"The way that I'm treating Cruise Control is this game is going to do roughly three times as well for us as a normal game, because we're making 100% of it," he says. "Normally we're taking a small cut of a game we're working with. Every sale of Cruise Control is worth three or four times as much to us. If we manage to make it do as well as one of our other games, that would be massive for us."
Cruise Control is No More Robots' first self-published title  |
Image credit:
No More Robots
If Cruise Control does well, Rose says that No More Robots might reheat the shooter that it was working on before. The company has a demo ready to go, but the version that makes it into the wild might be different and more scaled-back.
"I think that PvP shooters are not a viable thing for us," Rose says. "As a small company, to enter that space would be insane. I've started to think about repurposing it into a PvE thing."
Bloodbath
Looking back at the last few years in the games industry, Rose describes the scene as a "massacre". But No More Robots didn't grow significantly during the COVID video game boom – the reason being that expansion "scared the shit" out of Rose – and thus hasn't had to make the deep cuts that other companies have had to make since.
Rose fully admits that this was an "accidental" bit of "genius".
"At the end of 2021, I just split all the profits between all the staff," he says. "I gave our staff lots of money and rolled into 2022 thinking that that would just happen again. When it didn't, we were fine as we hadn't expanded. We just broke even again. We don't need to make loads of money, because who needs it? Everyone's getting paid. We're putting out a bunch of games; we're having fun. I know this sounds so naive and stupid, but somehow it's working."
Hypnospace Outlaw was an early hit for No More Robots  |
Image credit:
Tendershoot/Michael Lasch/ThatWhichIs Media/No More Robots
For the most part, No More Robots' publishing model hasn't changed much either. The label's megahit Descenders had a five-figure budget. The same is true for the majority of the company's games, including Hypnospace Outlaw and Yes, Your Grace. But a few games received larger budgets around COVID ("I did get caught up a little bit in what was happening," Rose admits), and No More Robots was "bit a couple of times for that".
Now, the company is firmly back to five-figure budgets, with the only exception being
Another Door
, an upcoming multiplayer roguelike with a budget of $180,000.
"I remember speaking to my wife, just saying that I was so sure about this one," Rose says. "She just said go for it. We just announced it, and it is popping. Obviously we still need to launch it. I'm hoping my intuition was correct on that one. But outside of that, our budgets have been low. They've been like five figures for the majority of games recently."
One reason Rose has been keen to stick with lower budgets is the unpredictable nature of the indie games business, where it's almost impossible to predict which games will blow up.
"I have to assume that every game will just do fine," he explains. "I have to assume that we're not going to be the flavour of the month; but if we are, that's fantastic. We just had
Thank You for Your Application
and were the flavour of the week. That was amaz
